title: Polynomial simplex complexity under zero-preserving perturbations
formal:
Does there exist one randomized two-phase simplex algorithm \(\mathcal A\), in the exact model below, and fixed integers \(C,k\ge1\), such that for every \(m,d\ge1\), every real matrix \(\bar A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), vectors \(\bar b\in\mathbb R^m,c\in\mathbb R^d\) with
\[
\max_{i\in[m]}\| (\bar A_{i,*},\bar b_i)\|_2\le1,
\qquad\|c\|_2\le1,
\]
and every \(0<\sigma\le1\),
\[
\mathbb E_{G,R}\,[T_{\mathcal A}(A,b,c,\sigma)]
\le C(m+d+\sigma^{-1}+1)^k?
\]
For each nonzero entry of \((\bar A,\bar b)\), independently add \(\sigma\) times a standard normal random variable; entries initially equal to zero remain exactly zero. The resulting data are \((A,b)\), and \(c\) is unchanged. The task is to solve \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb R^d\}\) exactly, including infeasibility and unboundedness. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions, centers, zero patterns and noise scales. Expectation includes both the perturbations \(G\) and independent algorithmic fair coins \(R\). This is an explicitly disclosed specialization of the source's general direction to the fixed artificial-variable initialization and fair-bit program class below. It is not a claim about every pivot rule, and the specified class is not asserted to include all published shadow-vertex implementations.
why: Zero coefficients encode much of the structure that makes large linear programs usable. A guarantee stable under preserving those zeros would test whether random-data explanations of simplex efficiency extend beyond dense perturbations. The question concerns the existence of an exact simplex implementation with a universal expected resource bound, and therefore separates a limitation of one pivot rule from a limitation of the whole specified algorithm class.

sentences: Smoothed analysis asks how a simplex algorithm behaves on a worst-case linear program after independent random perturbations.
This version keeps every original zero coefficient fixed and adds Gaussian noise only to nonzero matrix and right-hand-side entries.
The target asks whether some explicitly defined two-phase simplex algorithm solves every such family exactly in expected polynomially many arithmetic operations.
The algorithm class and additive noise convention are disclosed editorial choices completing a broader source question.
A complete Lean answer must prove the universal expected bound or refute it for every algorithm in the stated class.

definitions:
The notation \([r]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). A standard normal variable has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All perturbations are independent of each other and the algorithm's coins. No independence assumption is imposed on the entries of the fixed center. There is no bound on the number of nonzero entries per row: preserving sparsity here means preserving each prescribed zero entry. There is no conditioning on feasibility, boundedness or nonsingularity. The algorithm receives only \(m,d,A,b,c,\sigma\), not the center or the realized perturbation values separately.

Here is the precise allowed two-phase simplex class. All vectors and matrices below are formed after perturbation. Represent \(x=x^+-x^-\) with \(x^+,x^-\ge0\), introduce slacks \(s\ge0\), and let \(p=2d+m\). Let \(D\) be diagonal with \(D_{ii}=1\) if \(b_i\ge0\) and \(-1\) otherwise. Put
\[
E=D[A,-A,I_m],\qquad h=Db=|b|.
\]
The original problem has the standard-form constraints \(Eu=h,u\ge0\), where \(u=(x^+,x^-,s)\), and objective \(q^{\mathsf T}u\) for \(q=(c,-c,0_m)\). The structural identity matrix and the signs and duplicate columns introduced in this conversion are not independently perturbed. The matrix \(E\) always has row rank \(m\).

Phase I uses \([E,I_m](u,z)=h\), \(u,z\ge0\), and maximizes \(-\sum_i z_i\). It starts at the artificial-variable basis with \(u=0,z=h\). Phase II uses \(Eu=h,u\ge0\) and objective \(q^{\mathsf T}u\). A basis for a rank-\(m\) constraint matrix \(H\) is an ordered set \(B\) of \(m\) column indices whose matrix \(H_B\) is invertible. Its basic vector has nonbasic coordinates zero and basic coordinates \(H_B^{-1}h\); it is feasible when these coordinates are nonnegative. For current objective vector \(w\), the reduced cost of a nonbasic column \(j\) is
\[
\bar w_j=w_j-w_B^{\mathsf T}H_B^{-1}H_j.
\]
A legal improving pivot chooses a nonbasic \(j\) with \(\bar w_j>0\), computes \(v=H_B^{-1}H_j\), and, if some \(v_i>0\), exchanges \(j\) with any basic position attaining
\[
\theta=\min_{i:v_i>0}(H_B^{-1}h)_i/v_i.
\]
Ties may be chosen by the algorithm; \(\theta=0\) is allowed. The resulting basis must be the actual next basis. If all \(v_i\le0\), this column instead supplies a feasible unbounded improving ray. A basis with all nonbasic reduced costs nonpositive certifies optimality for its current phase. All computations to select a pivot, solve linear systems, check costs or maintain auxiliary data count toward the running time.

During Phase I only these improving pivots are permitted. If all artificial variables become zero, the algorithm may finish Phase I immediately, since the objective cannot exceed zero. It then removes basic artificial columns one at a time by basis exchanges with columns of \(E\), retaining a feasible basis with every artificial coordinate zero after each exchange. These cleanup exchanges need not have positive reduced cost; each must reduce the number of basic artificial columns by one. Once none remain, all artificial columns are discarded and Phase II starts from exactly that basis. If instead Phase I reaches an optimal basis with \(\sum_i z_i>0\), it returns infeasible. Phase II permits only the improving pivots just defined and ends with an optimal feasible basis or a feasible unbounded improving ray. No auxiliary constraints, additional variables beyond this initialization, jumps to a different feasible basis, changes to the objective within a phase, or interior-point moves are allowed.

An eligible algorithm is a single finite classical program with fixed rational constants. It must obey these rules, terminate and return a correct certificate on every real input \(A,b,c\) of the stated dimensions, every \(0<\sigma\le1\), and every sequence of coin outcomes. An optimum is returned as the final basic vector and basis; an unbounded outcome includes its feasible basic vector and improving ray; infeasibility includes the terminal Phase-I basis with positive artificial sum and nonpositive reduced costs. The representation \(x=x^+-x^-\) translates standard-form optimum points and rays back to the original problem. Arbitrarily small numerical gaps are handled exactly, with no feasibility or optimality tolerance.

The computation model has ordinary binary work tapes and exact real work tapes, all initially blank apart from the input. Dimensions are given in binary; real input data are stored in row-major order with dimensions delimiting the arrays. The program has finitely many heads and registers, independent of the dimensions. Each bit operation, fair-coin request, head move by one cell, real-cell copy/read/write, rational-constant load, real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and real comparison has unit cost. Branches use the comparison or bit outcomes. All instructions and memory access are charged. There is no integer-part operation on reals, transcendental-function primitive, infinite table, arbitrary real program constant, oracle, nonuniform advice, parallel processor, or free linear-system solver. Noise is sampled externally to form the input; its generation is not charged. This exact arithmetic model is specified because Gaussian input numbers have no finite exact binary encoding. The number \(T_{\mathcal A}\) is the total operation count, not merely the number of pivots or bit precision. Its expectation is an extended nonnegative real and may be infinite. The rational program constants, internal states and number of tapes are fixed once for \(\mathcal A\); the machine has no length-dependent advice. Internal coin requests read independent uniform bits from an infinite binary sequence.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete Lean proof of the displayed universal expected polynomial bound for some eligible algorithm, or of its full negation. A positive proof supplies one program and constants \(C,k\), establishes exact correctness and compliance with the two-phase pivot rules for every input and coin sequence, and proves the expectation bound for every permitted center and noise scale. A negative proof establishes
\[
\forall\mathcal A\text{ eligible}\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists m,d,\bar A,\bar b,c,\sigma\text{ as above}:\quad
\mathbb E_{G,R}T_{\mathcal A}>C(m+d+\sigma^{-1}+1)^k.
\]
The bad dimensions, center and noise scale may depend on the algorithm and proposed bound. A bad example for one pivot rule does not establish this negation. A theorem with dense noise, additional geometric assumptions, a different allowable algorithm class, or numerical feasibility tolerances must establish the full proposition above to count. This is an asymptotic resource question; the benchmark's numerical \(1/100\) acceptance tolerance does not weaken exact LP correctness or replace the polynomial bound.

context_blocks.text: Roughgarden explicitly identifies sparsity-preserving perturbations as a missing extension of smoothed simplex analysis in a footnote to the standard Gaussian model.
The source describes existing positive bounds for shadow pivot rules, while Spielman and Teng distinguish additive zero-preserving Gaussian perturbations from multiplicative relative perturbations.

This card chooses the additive model, fixed artificial-variable Phase I and a fair-bit program class with exact optimization; the original shadow initialization uses other auxiliary programs and continuous internal random vectors, so equivalence with that algorithm class is not asserted.
Bach, Black, Huiberts and Kafer's June 2026 revision explains why exponential examples survive zero-preserving perturbations for Bland's rule.
Their positive sparse-matrix analysis uses right-hand-side noise together with scaling parameters and numerical tolerances, so it does not by itself establish the universal exact statement here.
